content.title: About
content.content: Escargot are edible land snails that have long been a culinary delicacy, especially in France. They have a delicate, slightly nutty flavor and a tender, slightly springy texture. Escargot are commonly served as an appetizer and used in salads, pastas, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Escargot have been eaten since ancient Rome and Egypt.
France celebrates a "Fête de l'Escargot" dedicated to this delicacy.
Edible snails are farmed on specialized farms where their diet and environment are carefully controlled.
There are over 500 species of land snails, but only a few dozen are used in cuisine.
Traditional preparation involves cleaning, simmering in wine with herbs, then sautéing in butter with garlic and parsley.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Escargot provide about 13 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafood items, snails are low in fat and calories.

items.title: Source of iron and vitamin B12
items.content: They supply iron and vitamin B12, essential for blood formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals support muscle and heart function.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: A modest amount of omega‑3 contributes to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mollusks and snails.

items.title: Parasites
items.content: Raw snails can harbor parasites, so thorough cooking is required.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Traditional recipes often use salt and sauces, increasing sodium intake.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: Snails can accumulate toxins from polluted environments; purchase from reputable farms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Escargot are usually served as an appetizer: they are cleaned, simmered in wine with herbs, then sautéed in butter with garlic and parsley. They can be added to pasta, risotto, salads, or used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh snail meat should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days. Frozen escargot retain quality for up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw in the fridge before cooking and rinse under running water.
